spdx_id.description: The SPDX licence identifier the product is released under - `MIT`, `Apache-2.0`, `GPL-3.0-or-later` - or an SPDX expression where it is dual-licensed, such as `Apache-2.0 OR MIT`. It corroborates `free_and_open_source` and never decides it. OPTIONAL, AND IT IS THE ONE FIELD IN THIS BLOCK THAT CAN NARROW WHO IS ASKING. Single-vendor identifiers - `Zimbra-1.4`, `SugarCRM-1.1.3`, `Elastic-2.0`, `Motosoto`, `Naumen`, `iMatix` - are answered by approximately the products built on one vendor's stack, and one of those beside `platform`, `stacks` and `distribution_regions` can come close to naming the product. That happens by a truthful answer rather than by an attack, so nothing can prevent it. READ ONE DISTINCTION BEFORE DECIDING: an SPDX id names the LICENCE'S AUTHOR and not the declarant, so `Intel` here does not say the product is Intel's, and an identifier that names nobody - `MIT`, `Apache-2.0`, `GPL-3.0-or-later` - narrows to the products released under that licence and no further. The residual is in the single-vendor names above, not in the common ones. A COMBINATION CARRIES THE RESIDUAL OF EVERY OPERAND IN IT, because this field accepts expressions and not only single identifiers: `Zimbra-1.4 OR Elastic-2.0` says both of the things its two operands say on their own and so identifies more sharply than `Zimbra-1.4` does, while `MIT OR Apache-2.0` names nobody and carries no more residual than `MIT` does. It is the single-vendor operands in a combination that decide it, not the fact that it is a combination. WHERE THAT MATTERS TO YOU, OMIT THIS FIELD: `free_and_open_source` is what the licence half of both instruments' tests turns on, neither test asks for an SPDX identifier at any point, and omitting this costs the corroboration and nothing else. Omit it too where the licence is bespoke or proprietary - a `LicenseRef-` name is outside the vocabulary in any case. WHAT AN ACCEPTED VALUE LOOKS LIKE: one or more operands, each of them one of the 733 identifiers on the published SPDX Licence List, in the published casing (`mit` does not pass where `MIT` does), joined only by `AND`, `OR`, `WITH`, parentheses and a `+` suffix - the term after a `WITH` comes from the list's 86 published exception identifiers rather than from the 733 - and NO LONGER THAN 128 CHARACTERS IN TOTAL - the schema does not admit a longer truthful expression, though as the header says, nothing rejects one today either. Parenthesis balance is not checked and `(MIT` passes. WHAT IT DOES NOT SETTLE: it is not the free-and-open-source answer. `BUSL-1.1`, `SSPL-1.0` and `Elastic-2.0` are all on the published list and none of them is free and open-source software, because none provides all rights to use, modify and redistribute freely. That is exactly the corroboration this field exists for - it is the only thing in this block that can contradict a self-declared `free_and_open_source: true`.
spdx_id.$comment: WHAT FILLING THIS IN COSTS YOU, MEASURED RATHER THAN ASSERTED, AND THE MEASUREMENT CONTRADICTS WHAT THIS FIELD USED TO CLAIM. This profile's header forbids identifiers because it forbids saying what the code says. An SPDX id says how the product is RELEASED, which is a fact about the product in the same family as `platform` and `distribution_regions`, and the value is built only from published strings, with no free text in any position: every operand is one of the 733 published licence identifiers, optionally carrying a `+` suffix and optionally followed by ` WITH ` and one of the 86 published exception identifiers, and the operands are joined only by `AND`, `OR` and parentheses. An earlier version of this description went further and said the vocabulary "fingerprints nothing"; the independent check of 2026-08-05 falsified that by enumerating the accepted set, and the true statement is narrower. ACCEPTED IDS INCLUDE THE NAMES OF INDIVIDUALS, VENDORS AND PRODUCTS: individuals (`HPND-Markus-Kuhn`, `Brian-Gladman-2-Clause`, `Martin-Birgmeier`, `bcrypt-Solar-Designer`, `libutil-David-Nugent`), vendors (`Adobe-Glyph`, `IBM-pibs`, `Intel`, `Nokia`, `Xerox`, `MS-PL`, `RHeCos-1.1`, `FDK-AAC`) and products (`curl`, `Vim`, `PostgreSQL`, `OpenSSL`, `UnRAR`). THE DISTINCTION A READER NEEDS IS BACK IN THE DESCRIPTION AS OF 2026-08-05 - that an SPDX id names the LICENCE'S AUTHOR and not the declarant, so `Intel` on a profile does not say the product is Intel's. An independent check on that date found the alarming half of the residual had stayed in the description while the mitigating half had moved here, and that over-omission has a price, this being the only thing in the block that can contradict a self-declared `free_and_open_source: true`. WITHDRAWN IN THE SAME MOVE: the clause "`MIT` is true of millions of products and narrows nothing". Nothing had counted the products, and the description now makes the point without a number - an identifier that names nobody narrows to the products released under that licence and no further. The residual is real rather than theoretical, and it is the reason this field is optional. WHAT BOUNDS THE RESIDUAL, RESTATED ON 2026-08-05 BECAUSE THE BOUND THIS `$comment` STATED TWICE WAS FALSE OF THE FIELD AS SPECIFIED. It said "the value is one of at most 733 published strings". The pattern accepts EXPRESSIONS, so the accepted set is combinatorial over 733 operands and 86 exception terms rather than an enumeration of 733: measured on 2026-08-05, `Apache-2.0 OR MIT`, `(MIT OR Apache-2.0)` and `GPL-2.0-or-later WITH Bison-exception-2.2` all match the pattern and none of them is one of the 733, and the 128-character cap still admits 22 operands of the shortest published identifier - a chain of 22 `GD`s joined by " OR " is exactly 128 characters and matches, and a twenty-third takes it to 134 and fails `maxLength`; `GD` is one of the two shortest published identifiers, `SL` being the other, both two characters (independent check, 2026-08-05). WHAT SURVIVES IS CLOSURE AND NOT CARDINALITY, and closure is what the argument needed: every operand comes from a published list in its published casing, every joiner is `AND`, `OR`, `WITH`, a parenthesis or a `+`, nothing else matches, so no free text can be carried in any position. WHAT DOES NOT SURVIVE is the implication that the accepted values are the 733 identifiers, so the residual has to be stated over expressions and not only over single ids, where before this field warned about single-vendor identifiers and said nothing about combinations. WITHDRAWN 2026-08-05, THE SAME DAY IT WAS WRITTEN: the form that correction first took here read "a multi-operand expression is rarer than either operand alone and therefore narrows harder", and the description drew from it that "a dual-licence answer carries more of the residual above rather than less". Both are claims about how open-source projects declare their licences; nothing in this block has counted that population; and the second contradicted its own description two sentences earlier, `MIT OR Apache-2.0` being a common declaration whose two operands are named there as carrying no residual (independent check, 2026-08-05). The direction of harm was over-caution: a developer whose truthful answer is `MIT OR Apache-2.0` was told it is riskier than a single identifier and would omit it, losing the corroboration this field exists for. WHAT IS LEFT IS ABOUT THE VALUE AND NOT ABOUT THE POPULATION: an expression carries the residual of every operand in it, so a combination containing a single-vendor identifier carries that identifier's residual and a combination of common ones carries none. THE REST OF THE BOUND IS UNCHANGED AND STILL HOLDS. The value carries no free text, is chosen by the person rather than read from the tree, and no code path in this repository sends a profile anywhere: the CLI's only outbound request is a GET of a `--policy` URL the user names in `reconcile`, and it carries no profile (verified against `product/packages/cli/src/reconcile.ts` on 2026-08-05). THE PATTERN ENUMERATES THE VOCABULARY, AND NOTHING ENFORCES IT AT RUNTIME. Every operand must be an identifier on the published SPDX Licence List, joined only by `AND`, `OR`, `WITH`, parentheses and the `+` suffix, and nothing else matches - but see the schema header: no Ajv instance in this repository compiles this file, so a profile carrying `LicenseRef-Acme-Internal` is rejected by nothing and reported by nothing today. The guard is a SPECIFICATION until validation is turned on, and the confidentiality argument above depends on an enforcement that does not yet exist (independent check, 2026-08-05). The pattern shipped earlier on 2026-08-05 was a negative lookahead for `LicenseRef-` over an open character class, and an independent check measured it accepting `Acme Corporation Proprietary License`, `Palantir-Foundry-EULA`, `MIT (c) Hooli Inc`, `evil.com` and a lowercase `licenseref-acme` - the exact harm named above, reachable by not writing the one prefix the denylist knew. The property was asserted, not built; enumeration is what closed it. CASE. Only the canonical casing matches. The SPDX specification treats identifiers as case-insensitive for matching, so a truthful lowercase answer is a failure against this specification and not against SPDX. That is immaterial while nothing validates, and it is a reason to normalise case at whatever point validation is turned on rather than to reject. THE 128-CHARACTER CAP is a `maxLength` beside the pattern, and it was named in no part of this field's text until 2026-08-05, when an independent check measured a 145-character expression built only from accepted identifiers joined by " AND " being rejected by the full schema while the pattern alone matched it. The description now names it. WHAT THE PATTERN DOES NOT CHECK: parenthesis balance. A regular expression cannot count, and enforcing balance costs six copies of the identifier alternation instead of two. `(MIT` is a malformed expression that still carries no free text, and the vocabulary rather than the bracketing is what the confidentiality argument rests on - this is a vocabulary guard, not an SPDX parser. WHERE THE LIST CAME FROM, HOW IT AGES, AND WHAT MUST HAPPEN BEFORE VALIDATION IS TURNED ON. SPDX Licence List version e4c1f27, released 2026-07-16, from `github.com/spdx/license-list-data` - 733 licence identifiers and 86 exception identifiers, deprecated ones included because projects still declare `GPL-3.0` and rejecting a truthful answer is the worse error. It is a snapshot and it ages silently: a licence SPDX publishes after that date matches nothing here, and nothing in `npm run gates` notices, because `gates` runs offline and a network fetch inside it would make it flaky. It is the one check in this change that exists and is never run, and giving it a caller means adding a script to `package.json`, which is outside the files this change may touch (independent check, 2026-08-05). Without that, a developer who adopts an SPDX identifier published after the snapshot gets a bare pattern failure: a truthful answer with no way to express it and nothing telling them why. That is acceptable only for as long as the guard stays unenforced. IT IS ALSO THE ONE FIELD HERE THAT CANNOT BE WIRED TO A GATE LIMB, `declared_by` being read as a boolean - and that is true by silence rather than by refusal. `product/packages/cli/src/scope.ts`'s `atPath` returns `unknown` and the cast to boolean at its one call site is unchecked, so a string wired there would flow through, match neither `true` nor `false`, behave exactly as if absent, and nothing would report the mistake (verified against that file on 2026-08-05). TWO QUANTIFIERS WITHDRAWN ON 2026-08-05 BECAUSE NOTHING HAD MEASURED THEM. (1) The description said this was "THE ONE FIELD IN THIS PROFILE THAT CAN NARROW WHO IS ASKING". Measured that day, four fields elsewhere in this profile take arbitrary strings with neither an `enum` nor a `pattern` on them - `stacks[]`, `features.llm.providers[]`, `features.payments.provider` and `features.analytics_ads[]` - so the true statement is narrower: this is the one field in `supply` that can narrow, the other twelve being booleans. That does not soften the warning, because the vendor-named vocabulary is what the warning is about. (2) This `$comment` said "a minority of accepted ids name their licence's author". Nothing had counted that either, and it is not decidable without a rule for what counts as a name: measured on 2026-08-05 with a CASE-SENSITIVE prefix test, which is the rule this field itself imposes on an answer, 186 of the 733 published identifiers begin with one of the eighteen commonest licence-family prefixes (`MIT`, `BSD`, `Apache`, `GPL`, `LGPL`, `AGPL`, `CC`, `MPL`, `EPL`, `OFL`, `OSL`, `AFL`, `ISC`, `Artistic`, `Zlib`, `Unlicense`, `WTFPL`, `CDDL`) and 547 do not, and the 547 are a mixture of project, vendor and personal names with generic ones the prefix list does not reach. THE RULE IS NAMED BECAUSE THE SPLIT DEPENDS ON IT. This sentence read "188 ... and 545" and named no rule, and those are the case-INSENSITIVE numbers (independent check, 2026-08-05). Both are recorded: case-insensitivity adds exactly two identifiers, `zlib-acknowledgement`, which is genuinely a zlib licence that SPDX spells lowercase, and `mplus`, which is the mplus Font License and not an MPL-family licence at all - so the larger number also files one identifier under a family it does not belong to. The case-sensitive number is the sentence's, because a lowercase answer does not pass this field. The enumeration above is what the residual argument rests on and it needs no quantifier.

monetisation.description: Whether the product is monetised, and by which of the channels the two instruments name. Answer every channel you can. NO COMBINATION OF THESE ANSWERS IS A TALLY: both instruments' lists are open, one channel alone can be enough, and all-`false` here is not a finding that the supply is non-commercial. TWO FIELDS ASK THE SAME QUESTION WITH DIFFERENT SCOPE AND BOTH SHOULD BE ANSWERED - `by_the_manufacturer` for the CRA, which limits the question to the manufacturer's own monetisation because the CRA's free-and-open-source sentences in recital 18 do, and `by_anyone_including_third_parties` for the AI Act, which does not limit it because the AI Act does not. The remaining fields name individual channels in CRA wording, except `only_between_microenterprises`, which is AI Act wording. THAT IS ABOUT THE WORDING AND NOT ABOUT WHICH INSTRUMENT NAMES THE CHANNEL. AI Act recital 103 names four of the same channels in words of its own - a price, technical support or other services, a software platform, and the use of personal data - and it is wider than the CRA on two of them, which is why `paid_technical_support_beyond_cost_recovery` and `personal_data_required_as_a_condition_of_use` each say in terms that the AI Act answer is `by_anyone_including_third_parties`. The three the AI Act does not name at all are the donations channel, the cost-recovery fee and the not-for-profit carve-out: measured on 2026-08-05, "donation", "recuperation" and "actual costs" occur zero times in 32024R1689, as does every word beginning "profit". NONE OF THESE FIELDS IS WIRED TO ANYTHING as of 2026-08-05: adding the profile fields and making a gate consume them are two changes, and the second needs its own independent check.
monetisation.$comment: WIRING ONE LATER HAS THREE CASES, NOT TWO. `rules/gates/cra-scope.yaml`'s limbs carry three values of `closes_gate_when`, and which value a limb carries decides what a declaration on it can do. Measured against that file on 2026-08-05: 37 limbs, of which 21 `never`, 11 `"true"` and 5 `"false"`. The three lists below are NOT those 37. They are the limbs whose question a field in this block answers, which is a strict subset - the rest ask about product scope, sectoral exclusions, dates, addressees, or about facts no field here carries, `hosting-on-an-open-repository-alone` and `contributor-to-software-not-under-their-responsibility` among them. (1) `never`, which is safe: `price-charged-for-the-product`, `paid-technical-support-beyond-cost-recuperation`, `intention-to-monetise`, `personal-data-processing-required-as-a-condition-of-use`, `donations-exceeding-costs`, `donations-accepted-without-the-intention-of-making-a-profit`, `fee-charged-solely-to-recover-actual-operating-costs`, `product-is-free-and-open-source-software`, `component-intended-for-integration-by-other-manufacturers`, `component-monetised-by-its-original-manufacturer` and `not-for-profit-development`. A declaration on one of those annotates the verdict and cannot change it. (2) `"true"`, which needs care: `free-and-open-source-not-monetised-by-its-manufacturer` and `foss-component-for-integration-not-monetised`. A declared "true" closes the gate, which is why an exemption in that gate is claimed and never inferred. (3) `"false"`: `in-the-course-of-a-commercial-activity`, the limb this whole block most obviously answers. A declared "false" there closes the CRA gate, mediated rather than unconditional - `product/packages/cli/src/scope.ts` reports `contradicted-by-declaration` instead wherever the tree carries any contradicting commercial fact. AND THAT LIMB ALREADY CARRIES `declared_by: features.payments.present`; it was the only limb in the file carrying a `declared_by` at all when this was written, and `declared_by` is a single string, so pointing it at a field here would DISPLACE the payments answer rather than add to it. That is a behaviour change to the defect recorded in that limb's own note, not an addition, and it is one of the reasons the wiring is a separate change. CORRECTION HISTORY OF THIS MAP. The counts in the three lists were 10/3/1 when first written and are 11/2/1 as measured on 2026-08-05: `not-for-profit-development` was `"true"` until an independent check found that CRA recital 18 puts the not-for-profit carve-out on the DEVELOPMENT side while Art. 3(22) makes the SUPPLY the thing that must be commercial, so a not-for-profit that develops free and open-source software and then sells it answered that limb truthfully "yes" and took the whole instrument off a product the Regulation still reaches. It was demoted to `never` on 2026-08-05. Case (3) was not described at all by the earlier version of this map. An independent check on 2026-08-05 also found that the three lists named 14 limbs of 37 with no stated selection rule; the rule is now stated above. A MAP OF ANOTHER FILE'S VALUES IS A SECOND COPY OF A FACT TWO FILES MUST AGREE ON. Re-read `rules/gates/cra-scope.yaml` before trusting any of it, and do not take the counts on this page as current at any later date. NEITHER LIST OF CHANNELS IS CLOSED. What leaves the CRA's list open is "might be characterised", not the enumeration marker that follows it: recital 15 says commercial supply "might be characterised not only by" charging a price "but also by" the four others, and an enumeration of the form not-only-A-but-also-B-C-D-E does not by itself leave room for F, whereas "might" does. AI Act recital 103's list is open on its own face - "provided against a price or otherwise monetised, including through". `in-the-course-of-a-commercial-activity` is not the sum of these fields, and one channel alone can meet it.

by_the_manufacturer.description: Does the MANUFACTURER of the product monetise it - you, or whoever released it? Monetising covers charging for the product and the other channels the fields below name (paid support beyond cost recovery, an intention to monetise, requiring personal-data processing as a condition of use, donations beyond costs), and the list is not closed, so answer `true` for any other way the manufacturer takes money for it. THIS IS THE CRA'S QUESTION AND THE LIMITATION TO THE MANUFACTURER IS THE CRA'S OWN. Monetisation by an unrelated third party is `false` here. THE AI ACT'S VERSION OF THE SAME QUESTION IS `by_anyone_including_third_parties` BELOW AND IS NOT THIS ONE. Answer both. A `true` here means a `true` there as well; a `false` here leaves that one open. A `false` does not put the product outside the CRA. It is one cumulative element of an exemption whose other element is `licence.free_and_open_source`, and an exemption nobody claims is not an exemption.
by_the_manufacturer.$comment: THE NAME OF THIS FIELD IS THE CRA'S AND NOT THE AI ACT'S. Measured across the full Official Journal texts on 2026-08-05, `monetis*` occurs 7 times in 32024R2847 and twice in 32024R1689; the CRA names the agent three times and the AI Act names none. The CRA's three: recital 15's "by an intention to monetise, for instance by providing a software platform through which the manufacturer monetises other services"; recital 18's "the provision of products with digital elements qualifying as free and open-source software that are not monetised by their manufacturers should not be considered to be a commercial activity"; and recital 18's "should be considered to be making available on the market only if the component is monetised by its original manufacturer". Those are the Regulation's words, so under the CRA "by the manufacturer" is the provision's own limitation rather than a reading of it. WITHDRAWN ATTRIBUTION: an earlier version of this description put "that its manufacturer does not monetise" in the Official Journal's mouth. That is `rules/gates/cra-scope.yaml`'s own question wording and appears nowhere in the CRA - independent check, 2026-08-05, measured 0 occurrences in 32024R2847. THE AI ACT NAMES NO AGENT, AND CARRYING THE MANUFACTURER LIMITATION ACROSS TO IT WAS THIS REPOSITORY'S READING RATHER THAN THE AI ACT'S TEXT. WITHDRAWN WORDINGS: an earlier version of this description called the limitation "THE AI ACT'S OWN QUESTION" and said the CRA carried "the same limitation", which presupposed that the AI Act had one. The independent check of 2026-08-05 measured both `monetis*` occurrences in 32024R1689 and both are agentless, both in recital 103: "AI components that are provided against a price or otherwise monetised, including through the provision of technical support or other services, including through a software platform, related to the AI component, or the use of personal data for reasons other than exclusively for improving the security, compatibility or interoperability of the software, with the exception of transactions between microenterprises, should not benefit from the exceptions provided to free and open-source AI components", and "The fact of making AI components available through open repositories should not, in itself, constitute a monetisation." Neither says by whom. The vocabulary points the same way: the AI Act's actor is the PROVIDER and not the manufacturer - `provider` occurs 517 times in 32024R1689 against 9 for `manufacturer` - both counted as CASE-INSENSITIVE SUBSTRINGS, so `providers` and `Provider` are inside the 517, and the rule is stated because the number depends on it: measured on 2026-08-05 the case-sensitive substring count is 475 and the whole-word count 279, and the point holds on all three - of which 7 read "product manufacturer" and the other 2 refer anaphorically back to it inside one sentence of Art. 43. All nine belong to the safety-component regime for products covered by Union harmonisation legislation - recital 87, Art. 2(1), point (e), Art. 3(8), Art. 25(3) and Art. 43 - and none of them is in the free-and-open-source context. WHAT THE REPOSITORY'S READING COST, AND WHAT REPLACED IT. While this field carried both instruments, an AI component released under a free and open-source licence and resold by an unrelated third party with paid support answered "false" here, and on recital 103's literal words that component may nonetheless be one "provided against a price or otherwise monetised": a `false` claimed an Art. 2(12) exception whose literal words may not give it, which is the unsafe direction. (Recital 103's own word there is plural, "the exceptions", and the AI Act's enacting terms carry four; which of them this block reads the carve-back as reaching, and why that is a reading rather than a settled point, is recorded at `by_anyone_including_third_parties`.) The remedy in that version was an instruction to "record the downstream monetisation in words beside this answer rather than letting the \"false\" stand alone". THAT INSTRUCTION IS WITHDRAWN as of 2026-08-05: `supply` has no free-text field - twelve booleans and one identifier confined to a published vocabulary - and `additionalProperties: false` is set at every object level, so there was nowhere to record it and the `false` the caveat said must not stand alone stood alone (independent check, 2026-08-05). CORRECTION 2026-08-05: that sentence claimed the profile has no free-text field anywhere, which is false; the measurement is recorded at `supply`'s own `$comment`. The qualification is now carried as structure instead, by the sibling field `by_anyone_including_third_parties`, which asks recital 103's question with no agent in it. This field keeps the CRA's limitation because the CRA's own words impose it. WHY A CAVEAT WAS NOT ENOUGH ON ITS OWN. A person filling in a profile answers a boolean by reading its name; the independent check of 2026-08-05 measured the pre-split version of this description at 4,574 characters, with the contestability label roughly 55% of the way in, behind three earlier capitalised headings, and concluded that at that length the field name decides the answer. Splitting the field was that check's own recommendation. THE AI ACT IS WORDED MORE BROADLY THAN THE CRA ON TWO INDIVIDUAL CHANNELS TOO - see `paid_technical_support_beyond_cost_recovery` and `personal_data_required_as_a_condition_of_use` - and on both of those the AI Act answer is `by_anyone_including_third_parties`. THE CONTESTABLE READING IS NO LONGER CARRIED HERE. Before the split this field was in the class `rules/gates/cra-scope.yaml` applies to itself where a reading is contestable - recording a question rather than a settled reading - because it answered the AI Act as well. It now answers the CRA only, where the limitation is the provision's own words, and the contestable half sits at `by_anyone_including_third_parties`. Under the CRA it is the provision's own words. CORRECTION 2026-08-05, ON THE WORD "PASSIVE". The sentence above read "both are agentless passive" until an independent check found the second occurrence is the noun "a monetisation" inside an active clause - "The fact of making AI components available through open repositories should not, in itself, constitute a monetisation." Agentlessness is the whole of what the argument needs and is what was measured: the word "by" does not occur anywhere in recital 103, so neither occurrence attaches a monetising party to the verb. The same wrong characterisation stood in `by_anyone_including_third_parties`'s description as "worded in the passive throughout" and is corrected there too; measured on 2026-08-05, recital 103 has four sentences and two of them contain no passive construction at all.

by_anyone_including_third_parties.description: Does ANYONE monetise the product or its AI components - you, a reseller, a hosting provider, a distributor, or anybody else? Answer `true` if it is provided against a price by any party, or monetised through the provision of technical support or other services related to the product or its AI components (whether or not the charge only recovers costs), including through a software platform, or through the use of personal data for reasons other than exclusively for improving the security, compatibility or interoperability of the software. Making the components available through an open repository is not, on its own, monetisation. THIS IS THE AI ACT'S QUESTION AND IT DOES NOT SAY WHO DOES THE MONETISING. Recital 103 uses `provided` three times and `monetised` once, all four in its second and third sentences, and attaches an agent to none of them - the word "by" does not occur in the recital at all - so this field asks the question at its widest and does not stop at the manufacturer. It is therefore `true` whenever `by_the_manufacturer` is `true`, and it can be `true` where that one is `false` - a freely licensed component resold by an unrelated party with paid support is exactly that case. WHERE YOU DO NOT MONETISE IT YOURSELF AND CANNOT ESTABLISH WHETHER ANYONE DOWNSTREAM DOES, OMIT THIS FIELD RATHER THAN ANSWERING `false`. A published library can be resold, hosted or supported for a fee by parties you never hear from, and not knowing that is not a failure to answer: an omission claims nothing, while a `false` claims the Art. 2(12) exception on a fact you have not established, which is the unsafe direction. Nothing distinguishes a considered omission from a field nobody read - no object under `supply` declares a `required` array - so an absent answer must never be read as a `false`. A `true` costs an AI system the Art. 2(12) free-and-open-source exception unless `only_between_microenterprises` is also `true`. RECITAL 103'S OWN WORD THERE IS PLURAL - monetised components "should not benefit from the exceptions provided to free and open-source AI components" - and the AI Act has four, at Arts. 2(12), 25(4), 53(2) and 54(6). Art. 2(12) is the one this block reads the carve-back as reaching, because it is the only one of the four addressed to an AI system rather than to a model or to a supplier of components, and that is this block's reading rather than a settled one. A `false` does not deliver that exception on its own: a system placed on the market or put into service as high-risk, or falling under Article 5 or 50, is inside the Regulation however it is licensed. THE CRA'S SCOPE TEST takes no answer from this field; its question is `by_the_manufacturer` above. The CRA does turn on monetisation by parties other than the manufacturer in one other place, and nothing here is wired to it: its open-source software steward regime, defined at Art. 3(14) and imposing duties at Art. 24, reaches free and open-source products "ultimately intended for commercial activities, such as for integration into commercial services or into monetised products with digital elements" (recital 19).
by_anyone_including_third_parties.$comment: ADDED 2026-08-05, splitting the single field `by_the_manufacturer` in two, one per instrument. The reason is measured and is recorded in that field's `$comment`: the CRA names the monetising agent three times and the AI Act names none, so one boolean serving both either asserted an agent the AI Act does not name or carried a 726-word caveat that a person answering from the field name never reaches. WHY THE WIDEST READING. Under the AI Act a `false` on the monetisation question is a claim on the Art. 2(12) exception. If recital 103's agentless wording is read literally, monetisation by anyone at all defeats the exception, so a field that stopped at the manufacturer would produce a `false` that claims more than recital 103's words give - the unsafe direction. Asking the widest version and letting a reader argue it down is the safe one. NAMING. `monetised_downstream_by_others` was considered and rejected: it excludes the manufacturer's own monetisation, so a manufacturer who charges would answer it `false`, which is the unsafe direction again. This field has to be a superset of `by_the_manufacturer`, and its name has to say so without naming an agent the AI Act does not name. THE PROVISION. Recital 103: "For the purposes of this Regulation, AI components that are provided against a price or otherwise monetised, including through the provision of technical support or other services, including through a software platform, related to the AI component, or the use of personal data for reasons other than exclusively for improving the security, compatibility or interoperability of the software, with the exception of transactions between microenterprises, should not benefit from the exceptions provided to free and open-source AI components. The fact of making AI components available through open repositories should not, in itself, constitute a monetisation." Its first sentence sets the unit: "Free and open-source AI components covers the software and data, including models and general-purpose AI models, tools, services or processes of an AI system." WHICH EXCEPTION THE CARVE-BACK TAKES AWAY, AND WHY NAMING ART. 2(12) IS A READING. Recital 103's closing words are plural - "with the exception of transactions between microenterprises, should not benefit from the exceptions provided to free and open-source AI components" - and the AI Act's enacting terms carry four free-and-open-source exceptions, measured on 2026-08-05 as the only four articles in which "open-source" occurs at all: Art. 2(12) (the system is outside the Regulation), Art. 25(4), second sentence (a third party making tools, services, processes or components accessible to the public is relieved of the value-chain written agreement), Art. 53(2) (a provider of an AI model is relieved of two of Art. 53(1)'s obligations) and Art. 54(6) (a provider of a general-purpose AI model is relieved of the authorised-representative obligation). This block reads the carve-back as reaching Art. 2(12), because Art. 2(12) is the only one of the four addressed to an AI SYSTEM rather than to a model or to a supplier of components, and an answer in this profile describes a product rather than a model or a supply relationship. It is a reading and not a settled point: Arts. 53(2) and 54(6) state their own test, publicly available parameters, and recital 104 governs them; Art. 25(4) states its own, accessibility to the public, and carries no monetisation condition at all, `monetis*` occurring zero times in Art. 25 as measured on 2026-08-05. Every place in this block that names Art. 2(12) as the exception a monetisation answer bears on is using this reading, and each of them now says so (independent check, 2026-08-05). TWO CHANNELS ARE WIDER HERE THAN IN THE CRA, and that is why this field rather than the channel fields carries the AI Act answer on them. Recital 103 names technical support with no cost-recovery qualifier, so support charged at exact cost counts here and is `false` at `paid_technical_support_beyond_cost_recovery`. It names the use of personal data with no "as a condition for use" qualifier, so optional data use for other purposes counts here and is `false` at `personal_data_required_as_a_condition_of_use`. NOT WIRED to any gate limb, and deliberately: `rules/gates/cra-scope.yaml` is a CRA gate and this is an AI Act question. There is no AI Act scope gate in this repository as of 2026-08-05. WHAT TO ANSWER WHEN YOU CANNOT KNOW, ADDED 2026-08-05. An independent check on that date found this the one field of sixteen a reader could not answer from its description alone: the field's own premise is that monetisation by unrelated parties counts, a developer publishing a library cannot establish that, and two sibling fields - `only_between_microenterprises` and `fee_recovers_operating_costs_only` - state their own unknown case while this one did not. The only instruction that covered it sat two levels up in `supply`'s description, which a person filling in one boolean does not open. The description now says to omit rather than answer `false` where you do not monetise it yourself and cannot establish whether anyone downstream does - scoped that way because a manufacturer who charges knows the answer is `true` here whatever happens downstream - and omission is the safe direction here for the reason the whole field exists: under the AI Act a `false` on the monetisation question is a claim on the Art. 2(12) exception, so the unsafe answer is the confident `false`, never the blank. WHAT OMISSION STILL DOES NOT DO: it cannot be told apart from a field nobody read, no object under `supply` declaring a `required` array, so the description says an absent answer must not be read as a `false`. The same sentence, with its final clause adapted to which direction is unsafe, was added to the other two omit-rather-than-answer fields on the same day, closing an objection an independent check first raised against `only_between_microenterprises` and repeated when `fee_recovers_operating_costs_only` inherited the instruction. CORRECTED 2026-08-05: this sentence and its counterpart at `only_between_microenterprises` both said the sentence was the same, which is false of its ending (independent check, 2026-08-05). Measured that day, the first 169 characters are identical on all three descriptions; this field and `fee_recovers_operating_costs_only` end "must never be read as a `false`", and `only_between_microenterprises` ends "must never be read as an answer in either direction", because a `true` rather than a `false` is the unsafe answer there. The difference is deliberate and it is the claim of sameness that was wrong. WHY THE SUPERSET INVARIANT IS PROSE AND NOT AN ENCODED CONSTRAINT. The description states that this field is `true` whenever `by_the_manufacturer` is `true`, and nothing enforces it: measured on 2026-08-05, a profile carrying `by_the_manufacturer: true` beside `by_anyone_including_third_parties: false` validates against this schema under Ajv2020 in strict and in default mode. Encoding it would take an `if`/`then` pair, and this schema carries no keyword of that kind at all - measured the same day, `if`, `then`, `else`, `dependentSchemas`, `dependentRequired`, `allOf`, `anyOf`, `oneOf` and `not` occur zero times in the file, so every constraint here constrains one field's own value and none relates two fields to each other. Adding the first cross-field constraint changes what this schema specifies rather than how it is written, which makes it a granularity decision and the owner's; it is deliberately not taken here, and the independent check of 2026-08-05 recorded it the same way. The header's policy that every constraint is a specification is the argument for encoding it, and it is recorded here rather than answered.

price_charged.description: Is a price charged for the product? A `false` decides nothing on its own, and BOTH instruments are why: each defines making available on the market as covering supply "whether in return for payment or free of charge" - CRA Art. 3(22) and AI Act Art. 3(10), in the same words - so a free download is not outside either Regulation on the ground that nobody paid.
price_charged.$comment: CRA recital 15's first characterisation of supply in the course of a commercial activity, and the AI Act's "provided against a price" (recital 103). The quoted words in the description are CRA Art. 3(22), and the AI Act prints the same clause in its own Art. 3(10) definition of making available on the market, which is why the description names both: measured on 2026-08-05, "whether in return for payment or free of charge" occurs once in 32024R2847 and once in 32024R1689. An earlier version of the description credited the proposition to the CRA alone (independent check, 2026-08-05).

paid_technical_support_beyond_cost_recov.description: Is a price charged for technical support services in a way that does more than recover the actual costs of providing them? Support charged at cost is `false`. THE COST-RECOVERY QUALIFIER IS PART OF THE QUESTION and not an afterthought. THIS FIELD ANSWERS THE CRA ONLY. The AI Act names technical support with no cost-recovery limit at all, so a `true` here answers both instruments while a `false` answers only the CRA: support charged at exact cost is a `false` here and may still cost an AI system its exemption. The AI Act answer is `by_anyone_including_third_parties`. A fee charged to recover the running costs of a SERVICE that the product is delivered as part of is a different question, asked at `fee_recovers_operating_costs_only` below.
paid_technical_support_beyond_cost_recov.$comment: CRA recital 15's second characterisation, in its own words: "by charging a price for technical support services where this does not serve only the recuperation of actual costs". RECITAL 16 IS ADJACENT AND IS NOT THE CONVERSE OF IT, and an earlier version of this description said it was (independent check, 2026-08-05). What recital 16 says is: "Products with digital elements provided as part of the delivery of a service for which a fee is charged solely to recover the actual costs directly related to the operation of that service, such as may be the case with certain products with digital elements provided by public administration entities, should not be considered on those grounds alone to be a commercial activity for the purposes of this Regulation." That is a general proposition about a fee for a service, with public bodies as its example; it says nothing about technical support, and `fee_recovers_operating_costs_only` rather than this field is where it is answered. THE AI ACT IS WORDED MORE BROADLY. Recital 103 removes the exception where a component is monetised "through the provision of technical support or other services" with no cost-recovery qualifier at all. SO THE `true` DIRECTION ANSWERS BOTH INSTRUMENTS, AND THE DESCRIPTION DID NOT SAY SO UNTIL 2026-08-05. Support charged above cost is a fortiori support provided against a price, so a `true` here settles recital 103's channel as well and only a `false` is CRA-only. The structurally identical field `personal_data_required_as_a_condition_of_use` - where the CRA likewise adds a qualifier the AI Act does not have - had carried that sentence since an earlier round, this one carried the "THIS FIELD ANSWERS THE CRA ONLY" header without it and handled only the `false` case, and the sweep record at `supply`'s own `$comment` had called the two holding in the same way (independent check, 2026-08-05).

intention_to_monetise.description: Is there an intention to monetise the product - for instance by providing a software platform through which the manufacturer monetises other services? A free product given away beside a paid hosted edition is one shape it takes. HOW FIRM AND HOW NEAR THE INTENTION MUST BE IS NOT STATED BY THE PROVISION, and this block reads it as an intention you hold now about the product as you supply it today: a plan you have adopted and are acting on - a paid edition being built, a hosted service announced - is `true`, and a possibility you have not acted on is not. TWO THINGS A `true` DOES NOT SETTLE: whose intention it is, and which product it attaches to. A repository shipping a paid application beside a free library answers yes for the one and no for the other, so answer for the thing that is supplied. Financial support from manufacturers, contributions by manufacturers to the development, and regular releases are each expressly NOT grounds for a `true`, and CRA recital 18 is where that comes from: "the mere fact that an open-source software product with digital elements receives financial support from manufacturers or that manufacturers contribute to the development of such a product should not in itself determine that the activity is of commercial nature", and "the mere presence of regular releases should not in itself lead to the conclusion that a product with digital elements is supplied in the course of a commercial activity".
intention_to_monetise.$comment: CRA recital 15's third characterisation, in its own words - "by an intention to monetise, for instance by providing a software platform through which the manufacturer monetises other services". The AI Act names the same channel in recital 103, "including through a software platform". CRA recital 18 qualifies it twice and both qualifications cut against a "true": "the mere fact that an open-source software product with digital elements receives financial support from manufacturers or that manufacturers contribute to the development of such a product should not in itself determine that the activity is of commercial nature", and "the mere presence of regular releases should not in itself lead to the conclusion that a product with digital elements is supplied in the course of a commercial activity". THE TIME BOUND IS THIS BLOCK'S READING AND NOT THE PROVISION'S. Recital 15 says "an intention to monetise" and says nothing about when the intention must be held or how settled it must be. An independent check on 2026-08-05 found the field borderline for that reason - a developer who might charge one day had no rule - and the reading in the description was added to give one. A reader who disagrees with it is disagreeing with this block and not with the Regulation. WITHDRAWN 2026-08-05: the description called a free product given away beside a paid hosted edition "the ordinary shape". "Ordinary" is a claim about the population of open-source projects, nothing in this block has measured that population, and the identical test had already withdrawn "the single most common open-source shape there is" at `component_for_integration_by_other_manufacturers` on the same day (independent check, 2026-08-05). The example is kept and now reads as one shape the channel takes rather than as the usual one, because what it is doing is showing a reader what recital 15's clause is aimed at. THE POINTER TO THIS `$comment` IS GONE FROM THE DESCRIPTION, 2026-08-05: it said "see `$comment` for the two sentences that say so", and `$comment` is the one annotation no form generator, docs renderer or IDE tooltip shows (independent check, 2026-08-05). Both recital 18 sentences are now in the description itself, quoted from the Official Journal text of 32024R2847 and checked against it on 2026-08-05.

personal_data_required_as_a_condition_of.description: Must a user let you process personal data in order to use the product at all, for any reason other than exclusively for improving the software's security, compatibility or interoperability? THE EXCEPTION IS THOSE THREE PURPOSES AND NOTHING WIDER, read literally. A mandatory account whose data is processed for any other purpose answers `true`, and product analytics collected to improve features is such an other purpose. Answer `false` where the processing is optional, or where it is exclusively for those three purposes. THIS FIELD ANSWERS THE CRA ONLY. The AI Act carries the same three purposes with no "as a condition for use" qualifier, so a `true` here answers both instruments while a `false` answers only the CRA; the AI Act answer is `by_anyone_including_third_parties`.
personal_data_required_as_a_condition_of.$comment: CRA recital 15's fourth characterisation, in its own words: "by requiring as a condition for use the processing of personal data for reasons other than exclusively for improving the security, compatibility or interoperability of the software". A GLOSS THAT IS WITHDRAWN, KEPT HERE SO IT IS NOT REINTRODUCED: "something other than the software's own operation". It stood in an earlier version of this description, and it is NARROWER than the provision, because a product's own operation is wider than its security, compatibility or interoperability, so it answers "false" for a person the provision catches. AN INTERMEDIATE VERSION OF THIS DESCRIPTION GOT THE RECORD OF THAT GLOSS WRONG IN TWO WAYS and both are dropped (independent check, 2026-08-05): it quoted the gloss as "anything other than the software's own operation", a wording that was never used anywhere, and it asserted that the gloss still stood in another file's note, which was a claim about that file's current state and was untrue when written. The gloss is quoted above in the wording actually used. A THIRD CORRECTION, 2026-08-05. The version written to close the second one ended with the sentence "this description now makes no claim about what any other file contains today" while making one three sentences earlier, in a clause reading "which is the reading `rules/gates/cra-scope.yaml` announces and records as deliberate". The underlying claim was true when measured, but the description's account of itself was false, and it was the third consecutive round in which the closing statement of a fix did not hold. Both the clause and the closing sentence are gone: the description now states the literal reading and lets the provision govern, without reference to any other file. THE AI ACT IS WORDED MORE BROADLY. Recital 103 removes the exception for "the use of personal data for reasons other than exclusively for improving the security, compatibility or interoperability of the software" with no "as a condition for use" qualifier.

donations_exceeding_costs.description: Are donations accepted that exceed the costs associated with the design, development and provision of the product? That donations are solicited at all is not the question; the cost line is. WHETHER YOUR OWN UNPAID TIME COUNTS AS A COST DECIDES THIS FOR MOST SMALL PROJECTS, AND THE PROVISION DOES NOT SAY. A sponsor page taking EUR 3,000 a year against EUR 200 of hosting is `true` if costs mean cash spent and `false` if hundreds of unpaid hours are also costs. This block takes no position between the two readings, and the profile has no field to record which one was used. Where you must pick one: cash spent is the reading that answers `true`, and a `true` is one characterisation among several rather than a conclusion that the supply is commercial. ACCEPTING DONATIONS WITHOUT THE INTENTION OF MAKING A PROFIT IS A SEPARATE QUESTION and this field does not answer it. A surplus year at a project with no intention of making a profit is a `true` here and is not, on that ground, a commercial activity. No field in this block carries the intention question.
donations_exceeding_costs.$comment: CRA recital 15's fifth characterisation, in its own words: "by accepting donations exceeding the costs associated with the design, development and provision of a product with digital elements". TWO SEPARATE PROPOSITIONS, AND THIS FIELD CARRIES ONLY THE FIRST. Recital 15's closing sentence turns on intention and not on the cost line: "Accepting donations without the intention of making a profit should not be considered to be a commercial activity." The two do not cancel and neither answers the other - an earlier version of this description merged them (independent check, 2026-08-05). `rules/gates/cra-scope.yaml` kept them apart as two limbs when this was written and asked the second as `donations-accepted-without-the-intention-of-making-a-profit`; no field in this block carries it, so a project answering either way here should have that question put to it separately. UNPAID LABOUR. The provision says "the costs associated with the design, development and provision" and does not say whether the developer's own unpaid time is such a cost. An independent check on 2026-08-05 found that for the stated target user - a solo developer with a sponsor page, near-zero cash outlay and hundreds of unpaid hours - the two honest readings give opposite answers on the same project, and that 1,213 characters on this field did not reach the question. The description now states both readings, takes no position, and says which one answers `true`. THE AI ACT NAMES NO DONATION CHANNEL: searched the full Official Journal text of 32024R1689 for "donation" on 2026-08-05, zero occurrences.

fee_recovers_operating_costs_only.description: Is the product provided as part of the delivery of a SERVICE for which a fee is charged that serves solely to recover the actual costs directly related to operating that service? THE SERVICE FRAMING IS PART OF THE QUESTION. A bare cost-recovery charge for a download, not made as part of delivering a service, is `false`. WHERE NO FEE IS CHARGED AT ALL, OMIT THIS FIELD RATHER THAN ANSWERING `false`. The question is what a fee is for, so with no fee there is nothing to answer, and a `false` read against a product that charges nothing reads as a finding against it. Nothing distinguishes a considered omission from a field nobody read - no object under `supply` declares a `required` array - so an absent answer must never be read as a `false`. A `false` therefore means a fee IS charged and the condition is not met - either because it is not charged as part of delivering a service, or because it does more than recover that service's running costs. THIS ONE CUTS THE OTHER WAY FROM THE FIELDS ABOVE IT, AND A `true` IS NOT AN EXEMPTION. It removes one ground for calling the supply commercial and does not put the supply outside where some other channel is met.
fee_recovers_operating_costs_only.$comment: CRA recital 16 reaches "Products with digital elements provided as part of the delivery of a service for which a fee is charged solely to recover the actual costs directly related to the operation of that service, such as may be the case with certain products with digital elements provided by public administration entities", and such a fee "should not be considered on those grounds alone to be a commercial activity for the purposes of this Regulation". Read that qualifier in both directions: it is the reason a `true` here removes one ground rather than the question. AN EARLIER VERSION OF THIS FIELD DROPPED THE SERVICE FRAMING (independent check, 2026-08-05) and so asked a wider question than recital 16 answers. A DISCREPANCY THIS FIELD USED TO RECORD AGAINST THE CRA GATE IS CLOSED, AND THIS TEXT IS NOT A SUBSTITUTE FOR RE-CHECKING IT. An earlier version of this description said the limb `fee-charged-solely-to-recover-actual-operating-costs` asked a wider question, its wording lacking the "provided as part of the delivery of a service" element that this field carries. The limb's question was corrected on 2026-08-05 and carried the element when this was written, verified against that file on that date. The reconciliation went in this field's favour - the field stated recital 16 and the limb did not - so the field itself was unchanged by it. A change that wires this field to that limb must compare the two wordings at the time it is made rather than inherit this paragraph: what another file contains at any later date is not a fact this description can keep true on its own. THE OMIT-RATHER-THAN-`false` INSTRUCTION IN THE DESCRIPTION IS NEW ON 2026-08-05 and replaces an instruction that a report must say which of the two situations a `false` meant. `supply` has no free-text field - twelve booleans and one identifier confined to a published vocabulary - and `additionalProperties: false` is set at every object level, so the two situations cannot be distinguished in the answer; omission distinguishes them, and omission is available because nothing under `supply` is required, measured on 2026-08-05 as no `required` array on any object under `supply`. CORRECTION 2026-08-05: that sentence claimed the profile has no free-text field, which is false; the measurement is recorded at `supply`'s own `$comment`. WHAT OMISSION STILL DOES NOT DO, ADDED 2026-08-05: it cannot be told apart from a field nobody read. An independent check raised that against `only_between_microenterprises` and raised it again when this field inherited the instruction without answering it. The description now says an absent answer must not be read as a `false`, and so does `by_anyone_including_third_parties`, which gained the same sentence on the same day; `only_between_microenterprises` carries it with its final clause changed to "an answer in either direction", because a `true` rather than a `false` is the unsafe answer there. CORRECTED 2026-08-05: this sentence said all three gained the same instruction, which is false of the third one's ending, the first 169 characters being identical on all three and only the ending differing (independent check, 2026-08-05). THE AI ACT'S FREE-AND-OPEN-SOURCE PROVISIONS CARRY NO COST-RECOVERY LIMIT: searched the full Official Journal text of 32024R1689 on 2026-08-05 for "recuperation" and for "actual costs", zero occurrences of either. The heading is scoped to those provisions deliberately, having read as a statement about the whole Regulation until 2026-08-05 (independent check of that date): the AI Act does use cost-recovery language elsewhere, at Art. 58(2), point (d), "exceptional costs that national competent authorities may recover in a fair and proportionate manner", and at Art. 69(2), "the scale and structure of recoverable costs". Neither touches Art. 2(12) or recital 103, so nothing above changes.

not_for_profit_organisation.description: Was the product developed by a not-for-profit organisation that is set up in such a way that all earnings after costs are used to achieve not-for-profit objectives? BOTH ELEMENTS ARE REQUIRED AND THE PROVISO IS THE WHOLE OF THE TEST: a not-for-profit that may distribute earnings is `false`. IT IS ALSO CUMULATIVE WITH `licence.free_and_open_source`, as the CRA's two routes out are: recital 18's not-for-profit sentence reaches only the development of products "qualifying as free and open-source software", so a `true` here does nothing where that field is `false`. Whether an organisation is constituted that way is a fact about its articles, not about its code. Where the product was not developed by an organisation at all - a solo developer, an informal group of contributors - the answer is `false`. A FOUNDATION AMONG THE COPYRIGHT HOLDERS IS NOT A SIGNAL IN EITHER DIRECTION: the Free Software Foundation's own notice sits inside the text of the GNU licences themselves, so wherever one of those licence texts is shipped the Foundation is among the copyright holders, whoever wrote the product. THE PROFILE RECORDS ONLY THE YES OR NO: a `false` does not record which of the two elements failed, and there is no field for that. CRA ONLY - the AI Act has no not-for-profit carve-out.
not_for_profit_organisation.$comment: CRA recital 18's closing commercial-activity sentence, in the Official Journal's own words: "the development of products with digital elements qualifying as free and open-source software by not-for-profit organisations should not be considered to be a commercial activity provided that the organisation is set up in such a way that ensures that all earnings after costs are used to achieve not-for-profit objectives". CORRECTED 2026-08-05: the run-up to the quotation read "is not a commercial activity", hardening the recital's "should not be considered to be" into an assertion, and every other word of that run-up was the Official Journal's, so the line read as the provision (independent check, 2026-08-05). A recital's hortatory verb is not an operative one, and that difference is the difference between guidance and a rule, so it is restored. WITHDRAWN 2026-08-05: the instruction that "a report must name the failing element in words". `supply` has no free-text field - twelve booleans and one identifier confined to a published vocabulary - and `additionalProperties: false` is set at every object level, so there was nowhere to name it (independent check, 2026-08-05). CORRECTION 2026-08-05: that sentence claimed the profile has no free-text field anywhere, which is false; the measurement is recorded at `supply`'s own `$comment`. The description now says plainly that the profile records only the yes or no. THE AI ACT CARRIES NO NOT-FOR-PROFIT CARVE-OUT: searched for "not-for-profit", "not for profit", "non-profit", "nonprofit" and "no profit" across the full Official Journal text of 32024R1689 on 2026-08-05, zero occurrences of any of them. CORRECTION 2026-08-05, ON THE FOUNDATION SENTENCE. The description said the Free Software Foundation's notice "appears in every copyleft repository there is". That is false twice over and both halves were measured on 2026-08-05. Copyleft is wider than the GNU family: `MPL-2.0`, `EPL-2.0`, `EUPL-1.2`, `CDDL-1.0`, `OSL-3.0`, `Sleepycat` and `CECILL-2.1` are all on the published SPDX Licence List, all impose reciprocal terms on redistribution, and none of them is a Free Software Foundation licence. THREE RULES ARE STATED BECAUSE THE COUNTS DEPEND ON ALL THREE, and only the first was stated before 2026-08-05 (independent check of that date). THE DEPTH is the first: at full depth in the same trees the same measurement finds 438 such files, 27 naming a GNU licence of which 26 carry the notice, and 9 Mozilla Public License texts of which none does. THE BASENAME MATCH is the second: it is CASE-INSENSITIVE, because matching the uppercase spellings literally drops a licence file named in lower case. THE SCOPE OF THE NOTICE TEST is the third: it searches the WHOLE FILE, the GNU licence texts carrying the Foundation's address in their closing sections rather than in their headings. CORRECTED 2026-08-05: these counts read 8 of 8 at the root and 26 of 25 at full depth. They were produced by two different tests of what counts as a GNU heading - the file's own heading line at the root, the first 400 bytes at depth - and neither test was written down; the numbers above are all from the 400-byte test, which is the wider of the two. The conclusion holds under every one of the tests - the notice tracks the GNU licence text and not copyleft - and only the counts are rule-scoped. So the notice tracks the GNU licence text and not copyleft, which is the second half of why the original sentence was wrong. What holds, and what the point needs, is that the notice is inside the GNU licence text, so shipping that text puts the Foundation among a repository's copyright holders whoever wrote the product.

only_between_microenterprises.description: Does the monetisation you declared above consist ONLY of transactions between microenterprises - meaning that in every one of those transactions BOTH sides are microenterprises? YOUR OWN SIZE IS ONLY HALF THE TEST. A microenterprise employs fewer than 10 persons and has an annual turnover and/or annual balance sheet total not exceeding EUR 2 million; every party to the transaction has to meet that, not just you. If the product is sold to the public, or to anyone whose size you cannot establish, the answer is not `true`. WHERE THERE IS NO MONETISATION AT ALL, OMIT THIS FIELD RATHER THAN ANSWERING IT. It is an exception to monetisation and not a denial of it, so with nothing to except there is nothing to answer, and a `true` read over an empty set says the opposite to a reader of what it means. Nothing distinguishes a considered omission from a field nobody read - no object under `supply` declares a `required` array - so an absent answer must never be read as an answer in either direction. Answer it only where the AI Act is in scope and `by_anyone_including_third_parties` is `true`. Answering it does not turn that field over: it stays `true`. THIS FIELD ANSWERS THE AI ACT ONLY. It is the exception to the AI Act's monetisation carve-back, so a `true` restores the Art. 2(12) exception that monetisation had taken away - recital 103's own word there is plural, "the exceptions", and Art. 2(12) is the one of the AI Act's four that this block reads the carve-back as reaching. The CRA puts no equivalent exception on its commercial-activity test, and a CRA reader takes no answer from this field. THAT IS ABOUT THIS QUESTION AND NOT ABOUT THE WORD: the CRA defines microenterprises in Art. 3(19) by the same Recommendation, gives them support measures in Art. 33 and relieves them of certain administrative fines in Art. 64(10), point (a), none of which this field bears on.
only_between_microenterprises.$comment: AI Act recital 103, where this is the exception to the monetisation carve-back: monetised components lose the Art. 2(12) exception, "with the exception of transactions between microenterprises". Recital 103's own words are "the exceptions", plural, and fixing on Art. 2(12) is this block's reading of which of the AI Act's four the carve-back reaches; the reading and its reason are recorded at `by_anyone_including_third_parties`. THE THRESHOLD IS QUOTED FROM THE SOURCE RATHER THAN PARAPHRASED FROM MEMORY. Commission Recommendation 2003/361/EC, Annex, Art. 2(3): "Within the SME category, a microenterprise is defined as an enterprise which employs fewer than 10 persons and whose annual turnover and/or annual balance sheet total does not exceed EUR 2 million." The opening clause confines the definition formally to the SME category, and it was elided without an ellipsis until 2026-08-05 (independent check of that date; immaterial to the numbers). Fetched and checked 2026-08-05, after an earlier independent check recorded a paraphrase of it as unverified. The AI Act binds the term to that Recommendation in Art. 63(1), "Microenterprises within the meaning of Recommendation 2003/361/EC". BOTH PARTIES. Recital 103 says "transactions between microenterprises", which is a two-sided test, while this field's name and the single threshold quoted are both single-enterprise. An independent check on 2026-08-05 found that a solo developer reads their own headcount, sees "fewer than 10 persons" and answers `true`, and that nothing in 285 words said the counterparty's size was equally part of the test or what to answer when the buyer's size cannot be known. This is the one field in the block whose `true` RESTORES an exception, so a wrong `true` runs in the unsafe direction; the description now states both sides and the unverifiable-counterparty case. OMISSION RATHER THAN A VACUOUS `true` was added after an independent check on 2026-08-05 found two honest readers splitting between "true" and omission where there is no monetisation at all. IT SETTLES NOTHING UNDER THE CRA. The CRA does define the term, by the same Recommendation in Art. 3(19), but it puts no equivalent carve-back on its commercial-activity test and its scope gate had no limb for it: searched `rules/gates/cra-scope.yaml` for "microenterprise" and "micro-enterprise" on 2026-08-05, no match. WHAT OMISSION STILL DOES NOT DO, ADDED 2026-08-05: it cannot be told apart from a field nobody read, which is the objection an independent check raised when omission-rather-than-answer was first put on this field and raised again when `fee_recovers_operating_costs_only` inherited the instruction. Measured on 2026-08-05: no object under `supply` declares a `required` array, so both omissions are legal and neither is distinguishable from silence. The description now says an absent answer must not be read as an answer in either direction, and the same sentence with a different ending is on `fee_recovers_operating_costs_only` and on `by_anyone_including_third_parties`. CORRECTED 2026-08-05: this said it was the same sentence, which is false of the ending (independent check, 2026-08-05). Measured that day, the first 169 characters are identical on all three descriptions; the other two end "must never be read as a `false`" because a `false` is the unsafe answer there, and this one ends "an answer in either direction" because a `true` is the unsafe answer here. The difference is deliberate and it is the claim of sameness that was wrong.

component_for_integration_by_other_manuf.description: Is the product a component intended for integration by other manufacturers into their own products - a library published for others to depend on? An internal module of an application that is itself the product is `false`, because no other manufacturer integrates it. A `true` ALONE DECIDES NOTHING. It is the third cumulative element of the CRA's component route out, the other two being `licence.free_and_open_source` answered `true` and `monetisation.by_the_manufacturer` answered `false`. THE ROUTE OUT OF SCOPE IS THE CRA'S, AND THE AI ACT HAS A FREE-AND-OPEN-SOURCE PROVISION FOR THE SAME PARTY THAT IS NOT A ROUTE OUT. Art. 25(4), second sentence, disapplies that paragraph to "third parties making accessible to the public tools, services, processes, or components, other than general-purpose AI models, under a free and open-source licence", so the written agreement its first sentence otherwise requires with the provider of a high-risk AI system into which the thing is integrated is not required of them. It relieves one duty rather than putting the supplier outside the Regulation. ART. 25(4) ITSELF PRINTS NO MONETISATION CONDITION - measured on 2026-08-05, `monetis*` occurs zero times anywhere in Art. 25 - BUT DO NOT READ THAT AS AN ANSWER IF YOU MONETISE. AI Act recital 103 withdraws the benefit of "the exceptions", plural, from monetised free-and-open-source components; the Regulation's enacting terms carry four such exceptions and Art. 25(4) is one of them; and which of the four the withdrawal reaches is not settled, which is the open question recorded at `monetisation.by_anyone_including_third_parties`. A monetising supplier who takes the absence of the condition from Art. 25 as settling the matter may skip an agreement that is still required. ART. 25(4) IS ALSO WIDER THAN THIS FIELD, SO A `false` HERE DOES NOT CLOSE IT: its first sentence reaches a third party that supplies "an AI system, tools, services, components, or processes that are used or integrated in a high-risk AI system" - USED, not only integrated, and tools, services and processes, not only components - so a free-and-open-source tool or service that a provider of a high-risk AI system merely uses is inside that duty although no other manufacturer integrates it into their own product. This field and `licence.free_and_open_source` corroborate two of Art. 25(4)'s elements and settle it no more than they settle the CRA's route: Art. 25(4) also turns on the thing being made accessible TO THE PUBLIC and on its not being a general-purpose AI model, and no field in this block asks either.
component_for_integration_by_other_manuf.$comment: CRA Art. 3(6) defines a component as "software or hardware intended for integration into an electronic information system", and recital 18 narrows the carve-out further, to components "intended for integration by other manufacturers into their own products with digital elements". Recital 18 says the supply of such a component "should be considered to be making available on the market only if the component is monetised by its original manufacturer", which is where the third element and the cumulative reading come from. WITHDRAWN 2026-08-05: "THE AI ACT DOES NOT USE THIS ROUTE AT ALL", and the description's "CRA ONLY - the AI Act does not use this route" with it. Both were false and the independent check of 2026-08-05 found them in a node the round before it had edited. AI Act Art. 25(4), second sentence: "This paragraph shall not apply to third parties making accessible to the public tools, services, processes, or components, other than general-purpose AI models, under a free and open-source licence." Recital 89 gives its rationale and names the integration relationship expressly: "Third parties making accessible to the public tools, services, processes, or AI components other than general-purpose AI models, should not be mandated to comply with requirements targeting the responsibilities along the AI value chain, in particular towards the provider that has used or integrated them, when those tools, services, processes, or AI components are made accessible under a free and open-source licence." So the AI Act does address a free-and-open-source supplier whose component somebody else integrates, and it turns on two of the facts this block collects. WHAT ART. 25(4) DOES, PRECISELY, AND WHY THE ROUTE OUT IS STILL THE CRA'S. Art. 25(4)'s first sentence requires "The provider of a high-risk AI system and the third party that supplies an AI system, tools, services, components, or processes that are used or integrated in a high-risk AI system" to "specify the necessary information, capabilities, technical access and other assistance based on the generally acknowledged state of the art, in order to enable the provider of the high-risk AI system to fully comply with the obligations set out in this Regulation", by written agreement. CORRECTED 2026-08-05: the bridge between those two quotations used to read "to specify by written agreement the information, capabilities, technical access and other assistance needed", which dropped "necessary" and dropped "based on the generally acknowledged state of the art". The second is a LIMIT on the duty, so dropping it ran in the direction of a supplier owing more than Art. 25(4) imposes; both quoted spans were verbatim on either side of it and it was the unquoted bridge that lost the words (independent check, 2026-08-05). The second sentence disapplies THAT PARAGRAPH to free-and-open-source third parties; it does not disapply the Regulation. A supplier relieved of the written agreement is still inside the AI Act, whereas recital 18's component route, where it is met, means the component is not made available on the market at all and the CRA does not reach it. The two sentences also do not list the same things: the first names "an AI system" among what a third party may supply and the second does not, which on its face leaves a third party supplying an AI SYSTEM under a free and open-source licence outside the disapplication. That last step is a reading of the two lists and not a sentence in the Regulation, and recital 89 points the same way, listing "tools, services, processes, or AI components" and no AI system. Measured on 2026-08-05 and re-measured the same day by a method that ends an article at the next structural heading as well as at the next article: Art. 25 carries no occurrence of `monetis*`, so Art. 25(4) prints no monetisation condition of its own, and it carries exactly one occurrence of "free and open-source", in that sentence. THAT IS THE ARTICLE'S OWN FACE AND IT IS NOT AN ANSWER ON RECITAL 103. An earlier version of this sentence read "so unlike recital 103's carve-back this route has no monetisation condition", which decides the question this block records as open: recital 103 withdraws "the exceptions", plural, the enacting terms carry four, Art. 25(4) is one of the four, and which of them the withdrawal reaches is the unsettled point recorded at `monetisation.by_anyone_including_third_parties`. Nothing here decides it. The description carried the same assertion, unhedged, where a monetising supplier reads it, and both are corrected; the sweep that was meant to catch this class had been run by searching for "Art. 2(12)", which this field names nowhere (independent check, 2026-08-05). WHAT SURVIVES OF THE WITHDRAWN SENTENCE, because it was true of the provision it named: recital 103's "free and open-source AI components" covers the software and data of an AI system, including models, and carries no integration-by-others condition. Recital 103 is simply not the AI Act's counterpart to this field. Art. 25(4) is, and before 2026-08-05 this block cited neither Art. 25(4) nor recital 89 anywhere. WITHDRAWN 2026-08-05: the description called a published library "the single most common open-source shape there is". Nothing in this block had measured that, it is a claim about the population of open-source projects rather than about either Regulation, and no answer turns on it, so it is dropped rather than qualified. The example itself is kept, because what it is doing is telling a reader that a `true` here is ordinary rather than unusual.

annex_iii_use.description: Whether the product makes, or feeds, decisions in one of the AI Act Annex III areas this pack covers. ASKED, NEVER INFERRED. The same principle already governs `features.health_context` here, `in-the-course-of-a-commercial-activity` in the CRA gate, and the establishment limb of the DSA legal-representative checklist, whose row says outright that it 'is asked of the person running the scan and never inferred'. Article 6(4) is why an honest 'no' still matters: a provider who considers an Annex III system NOT high-risk must document that assessment before placing it on the market and is subject to the Article 49(2) registration obligation, so this answer selects which duty applies. It does NOT settle whether the Regulation reaches the product at all: Article 2(12) puts a system released under a free and open-source licence outside the Regulation unless it is placed on the market as high-risk or falls under Article 5 or 50, and recital 103 withdraws the benefit of the exceptions from a free and open-source AI component that is 'provided against a price or otherwise monetised, including through the provision of technical support or other services, including through a software platform, related to the AI component, or the use of personal data for reasons other than exclusively for improving the security, compatibility or interoperability of the software, with the exception of transactions between microenterprises'. THREE THINGS IN THAT SENTENCE WERE WRONG HERE UNTIL 2026-08-05 AND THE CORRECTIONS ARE THE POINT OF READING IT. Recital 103 says 'the exceptions', plural, and the enacting terms carry four for free and open-source AI - Articles 2(12), 25(4) second sentence, 53(2) and 54(6) - so rendering it as Article 2(12) alone, which this field did, understates what the withdrawal reaches; which of the four it in fact reaches is a reading and not a settled point, and it is recorded as such at `supply.monetisation.by_anyone_including_third_parties`. The personal-data channel was omitted here, and it is the one an ordinary product trips without charging anybody. The microenterprise exception was omitted too, and `supply.monetisation.only_between_microenterprises` exists to collect exactly that answer, so omitting it here left this description contradicting a field two nodes away. THIS FIELD IS ONE NODE OUTSIDE `supply`, AND THAT IS WHY IT WAS MISSED: the sweep that corrected these three things drew its boundary at the `supply` subtree by habit rather than by asking which nodes carry the proposition. That question is prior to this one; the ai-annex3-* checklists ask it separately and, as of 2026-08-05, `supply` above carries the declared answer to it. Corrected 2026-08-04 by the seventh independent check: this description ended "never whether there is one", which is the exact proposition Article 2(12) refutes, and it was written the same day the provision was added to those four checklists.
